courseTitle: How IT Teams Work: Agile, Waterfall, Scrum, Kanban & Software Releases

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one real cloud-infrastructure request (standing up a new VPC/VNet for a project team, migrating a database to a managed cloud service, or adding a CDN in front of a slow site). Sketch a one-page delivery plan for it twice: once as a Waterfall project with the 6 phases (Requirements, Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, Maintenance) each given a fixed duration, and once as an Agile plan broken into three 1-week sprints with a one-sentence infrastructure goal per sprint. Write 2-3 sentences explaining which model you'd actually recommend for this specific infrastructure change and why.
slots.deliverable: A one-page written comparison showing the same infrastructure change planned under Waterfall's 6 phases and under 3 Agile sprints, plus a short recommendation with reasoning.

slots.practicalActivity: For the same cloud project from the last session, write 4 user stories in the "As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]" shape — at least one written from the perspective of an application team that depends on your infrastructure, not just "as a cloud engineer." Give each story at least 2 specific, checkable acceptance criteria (not vague ones like "the environment works"). Then assign the three Scrum roles (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers) to yourself and two imaginary teammates, and write a 3-sentence Sprint Planning summary stating the sprint goal and which of your 4 stories you'd pull into a one-week sprint.
slots.deliverable: 4 written user stories with acceptance criteria, plus a short Sprint Planning summary naming the sprint goal and the stories committed to it.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a real Kanban board for your cloud project's 4 user stories, either on paper, in a spreadsheet, or in a free tool (Trello, GitHub Projects, or Jira's free tier) with columns Backlog, To Do, In Progress, Review, Done. Break each story into 2-3 smaller task cards (8-12 cards total — things like "provision subnet," "attach security group," "write Terraform module," "open firewall rule"), set a WIP limit of 3 on "In Progress," and move at least 3 cards through two columns to simulate a day of work. Mark one card "Blocked" with a one-sentence reason (e.g. waiting on a change-advisory approval or a quota increase).
slots.deliverable: A working Kanban board (screenshot or photo) with at least 8 task cards distributed across its columns, a visible WIP limit on In Progress, and one card marked Blocked with a stated reason.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one of your infrastructure stories and write a short narrative tracing it through Dev, QA, UAT, and Production exactly as the lesson's ticket-journey diagram lays it out — but for infrastructure, not application code: who picks up the ticket, what a peer review of an IaC change (Terraform/Bicep/CloudFormation plan) would check, what a QA pass would verify in a sandbox or staging subscription (including one edge case, like a region or AZ outage), what the business or application owner would check in UAT, and what "deployed" means for this specific infrastructure change. Then write one sentence for each environment naming the specific question it answers.
slots.deliverable: A written walkthrough of one infrastructure change through all 4 environments (Dev, QA, UAT, Production), with the owner and the specific question answered at each stage.

slots.practicalActivity: Install Git if needed, run git init to create a real local repository for your infrastructure project, add a .gitignore (exclude .tfstate and any credentials files), and make 3 real commits with specific messages (not "fixed stuff") as you add a README and two placeholder files representing infrastructure-as-code modules (e.g. a stub network.tf and a stub compute.tf). Create a branch named add-network-module, commit on it, then merge it back. If you have a GitHub account, push the repo and open a pull request for the branch before merging it there instead.
slots.deliverable: A real local (or GitHub) Git repository with a .gitignore, at least 3 commits with specific messages, and one branch that was created, committed to, and merged.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a release checklist for rolling out your project's first infrastructure change (e.g. a new network rule, a scaled-up compute tier, or a new managed database instance), covering all four required items: Approval (who signs off on a production infrastructure change), Monitoring (what metrics or alerts you'd watch after it goes live — latency, error rate, resource utilization), Rollback plan (the specific way to revert it, such as re-applying a prior Terraform state or restoring from a snapshot), and Release notes (a real, specific note like the lesson's example, not "various improvements"). Then pick one deployment strategy (blue-green, canary, rolling, or feature flag) that fits rolling out an infrastructure change and write 2-3 sentences justifying the choice over the other three.
slots.deliverable: A written release checklist (approval, monitoring, rollback plan, release notes) for one infrastructure change, plus a justified choice of deployment strategy.

slots.practicalActivity: Work through the full Castlebridge Retail capstone scenario from the lesson, but read it with a cloud-infrastructure lens: write 3+ user stories (revenue-by-region, revenue-by-category, automatic refresh) with acceptance criteria, treating the "automatic refresh" story as the infrastructure piece — what compute, network, and scheduling pieces would actually need to exist for it to run unattended at 7 AM. Build a 5-column Kanban board and place the stories on it, write a short QA test plan including the zero-sales edge case, write a one-paragraph UAT sign-off in the sales director's voice, write a specific release note, and write how you'd investigate and communicate about the simulated production incident where a region shows zero sales two days after launch — including which piece of infrastructure (a scheduled job, a network path, a permissions boundary) you'd check first.
slots.deliverable: A complete capstone packet: 3+ user stories with acceptance criteria, a Kanban board, a QA test plan with an edge case, a UAT sign-off, release notes, and a written incident-response plan for the zero-sales scenario.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: A student finishing this course can step into any IT or infrastructure team's real workflow on day one — writing real user stories for an infrastructure change, working a Kanban board, understanding why a network or compute change passes through Dev/QA/UAT/Production before it ever touches real users, using Git's clone-branch-commit-push-PR cycle on infrastructure-as-code, and reasoning about a CI/CD release, rollback plan, and production incident the way a cloud engineer actually has to.
